justice: The street allocates substantial space to planting strips, hedges, and residential setbacks, but there is no clearly dedicated sidewalk visible for pedestrians, so spatial resources are not evenly balanced across users.

A three-wheeled motor vehicle occupies the middle of a narrow shared roadway while several pedestrians walk directly in the carriageway, indicating that vulnerable users and vehicles are not given equally protected space.
The road edges are bounded by curbs, hedges, fences, and dense vegetation, and no marked barrier-free route or curb ramp is visible, which limits universal accessibility for all social groups.
safety: Pedestrians are walking in the same narrow lane as a moving three-wheeled vehicle, creating direct conflict between walking and driving movements.
The building on the right is under construction with visible scaffolding and several workers gathered near the frontage, which introduces potential falling-object and obstruction risks.
The curved alignment of the lane reduces forward visibility, and the landscaping plus parked or standing activity near the bend may further limit reaction time for all road users.
livability: The street has abundant greenery, including mature trees, hedges, and dense planting, which improves the residential atmosphere and environmental quality.
Multiple people are present outdoors and interacting near the building frontage, suggesting some level of social activity and neighborhood use.
The setting appears residential and relatively low-speed, but the lack of clear pedestrian realm and the active construction site reduce everyday convenience and ease of use.
sustainability: The corridor includes extensive trees, shrubs, and planted edges, indicating strong green infrastructure compared with a fully paved street.
The narrow roadway and residential scale suggest a lower-speed, lower-capacity environment that may generate less car-dominated traffic than a wide urban road.
No dedicated bike lane, bus stop, or visible public transport facility is present, so sustainable mobility support is only partial despite the strong vegetation.
aesthetics: Lush street trees and hedge planting create a visually green and pleasant streetscape.
The residential buildings have a relatively orderly massing and clean facades, which contributes to visual coherence.
The scaffolding, construction materials, and work activity on the right side interrupt the otherwise attractive scene and reduce visual neatness.
comfort: Tree canopies and dense vegetation on both sides provide meaningful shade, improving thermal comfort in sunny conditions.
The roadway surface appears smooth and well maintained, which supports physical comfort for slow vehicle travel and careful walking.
There are no visible benches, rest areas, or separated pedestrian walking zones, so comfort is limited for people who need a protected or stationary place to pause.
Because pedestrians share space with vehicles and construction activity, psychological comfort is reduced even though the street is green and relatively calm.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is clearly visible, forcing pedestrians to walk within the vehicular lane.
The narrow curved road lacks marked crossings or pedestrian-priority treatments, weakening route clarity and pedestrian protection.
Vegetation and a low-speed residential character support a somewhat pleasant walking environment, but the absence of dedicated walking infrastructure substantially lowers walkability.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane, cycle track, or bicycle priority marking anywhere on the roadway.
Cyclists would need to share a narrow curved lane with a motorized three-wheeler and pedestrians, creating multiple conflict points.
No bicycle parking, wayfinding, or intersection treatments for cycling are visible, so the street offers very limited dedicated support for bike use.
